concepts: Union of sets and counting elements by double counting
questions.question: Let $\bigcup_{i=1}^{50}X_i=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}Y_i=T$, where each $X_i$ contains 10 elements and each $Y_i$ contains 5 elements. If each element of the set $T$ is an element of exactly 20 of the sets $X_i$'s and exactly 6 of the sets $Y_i$'s, then $n$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Count the (set, element) incidences two ways: sets $\times$ size $=|T|\times$ multiplicity.
solution: Number of elements in $T$ from the $X$-family: $\sum|X_i|=50\times10=500$ incidences.
Each element of $T$ lies in exactly 20 of the $X_i$, so $|T|=\frac{50\times10}{20}=25$.
From the $Y$-family: $\sum|Y_i|=n\times5$ incidences, and each element lies in exactly 6 of the $Y_i$, so $|T|=\frac{n\times5}{6}$.
useful_results: Double counting: if every element of $T$ lies in exactly $m$ of $k$ sets of size $s$, then $|T|=\frac{ks}{m}$.
The same principle gives the handshake lemma ($\sum\deg=2E$) and the count of point-line incidences.
Here the two families give $\frac{50\cdot10}{20}=\frac{n\cdot5}{6}$, so $n=\frac{6\cdot25}{5}=30$.

concepts: Domain of a composite function
Limit of a rational function (removable discontinuity)
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\sin^{-1}x$ and $g(x)=\frac{x^2-x-2}{2x^2-x-6}$. If $g(2)=\lim_{x\to2}g(x)$, then the domain of the function $f\circ g$ is:
questions.key_idea: $f\circ g$ is defined exactly when $-1\le g(x)\le1$; first remove the common factor $(x-2)$ to get $g$.
solution: At $x=2$: $g(2)=\frac37\in[-1,1]$, so $f\circ g$ is defined at $x=2$ ...(i)
Sign scheme: first inequality gives $x<-\frac32$ or $x\ge-\frac43$; second gives $x\le-2$ or $x>-\frac32$.
Using (i) and (ii), the domain of $f\circ g$ is $(-\infty,-2]\cup\left[-\frac43,\infty\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $g=\frac12-\frac{1}{2w}$ with $w=2x+3$; then $|g|\le1$ becomes a condition on $\frac1w$ alone.
solution: $\frac1w\ge-1$: for $w>0$ always true; for $w<0$ it needs $w\le-1$.
$\frac1w\le3$: for $w<0$ always true; for $w>0$ it needs $w\ge\frac13$.
$x=2$ is included since $g(2)=\frac37$, and it already lies in $x\ge-\frac43$. Domain: $(-\infty,-2]\cup\left[-\frac43,\infty\right)$.

useful_results: $\sin^{-1}(g(x))$ and $\cos^{-1}(g(x))$ are defined iff $|g(x)|\le1$; $\tan^{-1}$ has no restriction.
A linear fractional function $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ equals constant $+\frac{k}{cx+d}$; inequalities on it reduce to inequalities on $\frac1w$ (a hyperbola).
$-1\le\frac{p}{q}\le1\iff\frac{p+q}{q}\ge0$ and $\frac{q-p}{q}\ge0$; solve with a sign (wavy-curve) scheme and intersect.
Check the point where the formula is redefined (here $x=2$) separately - the removable point may or may not belong to the domain.

concepts: Limit of a sum involving the greatest integer function (sandwich theorem)
questions.question: The value of $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{[r]+[2r]+\dots+[nr]}{n^2}$, where $r$ is a non-zero real number and $[r]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $r$, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Use $x-1<[x]\le x$ for each term and sandwich the sum between two quantities with the same limit.
solution: By the sandwich concept, use $x-1<[x]\le x$.
As $n\to\infty$: left side $\to\frac r2-0=\frac r2$ (since $\frac{n}{n^2}\to0$) and right side $\to\frac r2$.
By the sandwich theorem the limit is $\frac r2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Stolz-Cesaro: for $\frac{a_n}{b_n}$ with $b_n=n^2$ strictly increasing to $\infty$, the limit equals $\lim\frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n}$.
solution: Let $a_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}[kr]$ and $b_n=n^2$; $b_n$ is strictly increasing and unbounded.
Both bounds $\to\frac r2$ as $n\to\infty$, so $\lim\frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n}=\frac r2$.

useful_results: $[x]=x-\{x\}$ with $0\le\{x\}<1$, so $\sum_{k=1}^{n}[kx]=x\frac{n(n+1)}{2}-O(n)$; the fractional parts never matter after dividing by $n^2$.
Generalisation: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n^{p+1}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}[k^pr]$-type sums behave like the integral $\int_0^1 rx^p\,dx$ (here $\int_0^1 rx\,dx=\frac r2$).
Stolz-Cesaro: $\lim\frac{a_n}{b_n}=\lim\frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n}$ when $b_n\uparrow\infty$ and the right limit exists (the discrete L'Hopital).

concepts: Equal ratios with inverse trigonometric functions
$\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac\pi2$ and double-angle identity for cosine
questions.question: If $\frac{\sin^{-1}x}{a}=\frac{\cos^{-1}x}{b}=\frac{\tan^{-1}y}{c}$; $0<x<1$, then the value of $\cos\left(\frac{\pi c}{a+b}\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Put the common ratio $=K$, then $a+b=\frac{\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x}{K}=\frac{\pi}{2K}$ eliminates $x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test with a convenient admissible data set and eliminate options numerically.
solution: Then $\frac{\pi c}{a+b}=\frac\pi3$ and the required value is $\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12$.
Only (D) gives $\frac12$ (and the choice $c=1$, $y=1$ gives $0$ for all four, so it would not discriminate).

useful_results: $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac\pi2$ for $x\in[-1,1]$; $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac\pi2$ for all real $x$.
For a chain of equal ratios $\frac{p}{a}=\frac{q}{b}=\frac{r}{c}=K$, always introduce $K$: sums and combinations of $a,b,c$ become the same combination of $p,q,r$ divided by $K$.
When a question has a unique option, choosing one admissible numerical instance is a valid cross-check (use two instances if the first makes several options coincide).

concepts: Counting elements of a relation on $A\times B$ defined by divisibility
questions.question: Let $A=\{2,3,4\}$ and $B=\{8,9,12\}$. Then the number of elements in the relation $R=\{((a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2))\in(A\times B,A\times B):a_1\text{ divides }b_2\text{ and }a_2\text{ divides }b_1\}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The two divisibility conditions involve disjoint pairs $(a_1,b_2)$ and $(a_2,b_1)$, so they are independent: count = (number of valid pairs)$^2$.
solution: Similarly $a_2\in A,\ b_1\in B$ with $a_2\mid b_1$: the same 6 possibilities for $(a_2,b_1)$.
The choice of $(a_1,b_2)$ and the choice of $(a_2,b_1)$ are independent, and together they determine $((a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2))$ uniquely.
useful_results: If a relation on $X\times Y$ is defined by two conditions on disjoint coordinate pairs, the count is the product of the counts: $|R|=|S|^2$ when both conditions use the same set $S$ of pairs.
The number of $(a,b)\in A\times B$ with $a\mid b$ is $\sum_{a\in A}\#\{\text{multiples of }a\text{ in }B\}$; here each of $2,3,4$ has exactly two multiples in $B$, giving $3\times2=6$.
List divisor pairs systematically (by $a$) to avoid omissions.

concepts: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties of a relation on $\mathbb Z$ (gcd condition)
questions.question: The relation $R=\{(a,b):\gcd(a,b)=1,\ 2a\neq b,\ a,b\in\mathbb Z\}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Each property fails by one explicit counterexample; the extra condition $2a\neq b$ is what breaks symmetry and transitivity.
solution: Reflexive: for $a=2$, $\gcd(2,2)=2\neq1$, so $(2,2)\notin R$; in general $\gcd(a,a)=|a|$. So $R$ is not reflexive.
Symmetric: $\gcd(a,b)=1\Rightarrow\gcd(b,a)=1$, but the condition $2a\neq b$ is not symmetric.
Counterexample: $(2,1)\in R$ since $\gcd(2,1)=1$ and $2\cdot2=4\neq1$; but $(1,2)\notin R$ since $2\cdot1=2=b$. So $R$ is not symmetric.
But $(1,2)\notin R$ because $2\cdot1=2$. So $R$ is not transitive.
Hence $R$ is neither symmetric nor transitive (and not reflexive): option (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF checks only reflexivity (correctly: not reflexive) and then claims 'gcd(b,a)=1 so R is symmetric on Z', which ignores the condition 2a != b; R is NOT symmetric ((2,1) in R, (1,2) not in R). The PDF never examines transitivity. Its final key D is right, but its working proves the wrong thing; the symmetric and transitive counterexamples above were added.
useful_results: To refute a property, give one explicit counterexample; to prove it, argue for all elements. A condition such as $2a\neq b$ that is not symmetric in $(a,b)$ immediately kills symmetry.
A relation is an equivalence relation iff it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; check reflexivity first (here $\gcd(a,a)=|a|$ fails for $a\neq\pm1$).
Failing transitivity: look for a chain $a\,R\,b\,R\,c$ with $a\,R\,c$ broken by the extra condition (here $b=3$ links $1$ to $2$, but $2\cdot1=2$).

concepts: Functional equation with a cyclic substitution
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb R-\{0,1\}\to\mathbb R$ be a function such that $f(x)+f\left(\frac1{1-x}\right)=1+x$. Then $f(2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The map $x\mapsto\frac1{1-x}$ has period 3 ($2\to-1\to\frac12\to2$), so three substitutions give three linear equations.

solution: Add the first and third, subtract the second: $2f(x)=(1+x)+(1+T^2x)-(1+Tx)$.

useful_results: A Mobius map of finite order (such as $x\mapsto\frac1{1-x}$ of order 3 or $x\mapsto\frac1x$ of order 2) lets you generate a closed system of equations by substituting along its orbit.
For $f(x)+f(Tx)=g(x)$ with $T^3=\mathrm{id}$: $f(x)=\frac12\left[g(x)-g(Tx)+g(T^2x)\right]$.
Always verify that the orbit stays in the domain (here $\{2,-1,\tfrac12\}$ avoids $0$ and $1$).

concepts: Additive-recurrence function on $\mathbb N$
One-one and onto properties of composite functions
questions.question: Let $f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that $f(n+1)=f(n)+f(1)\ \forall n\in\mathbb N$ and $g$ be any arbitrary function. Which of the following statements is NOT true?
options: If $g$ is onto, then $f\circ g$ is one-one
If $f$ is onto, then $f(n)=n\ \forall n\in\mathbb N$
If $f\circ g$ is one-one, then $g$ is one-one
questions.answer: (A) If $g$ is onto, then $f\circ g$ is one-one
questions.key_idea: The recurrence forces $f(n)=nf(1)$; then $f$ is one-one, and a composite $f\circ g$ is one-one only if $g$ is.
solution: Then $f(3)=f(2)+f(1)=3f(1)$ and $f(4)=4f(1)$; by induction $f(n)=nf(1)$ for all $n\in\mathbb N$.
(A): if $g$ is onto, $f\circ g$ need not be one-one. Example: $f(n)=n$ and $g(n)=\lceil n/2\rceil$ is onto but not one-one, so $f\circ g=g$ is not one-one. So (A) is NOT true.
(B): if $f$ is onto, $1$ must be in the range; $f(n)=nf(1)=1$ with $f(1)\ge1$ forces $n=1$ and $f(1)=1$. So $f(n)=n$ (check: $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=2$, $f(3)=3$). True.
(C): if $f\circ g$ is one-one, then $g(a)=g(b)\Rightarrow f(g(a))=f(g(b))\Rightarrow a=b$, so $g$ is one-one. True.
(D): $f(n)=nf(1)$ with $f(1)\ge1$ is strictly increasing, so $f$ is one-one. True.
Hence the statement that is NOT true is (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working has typos (writes 'f(4) = 4 + (1)' for f(4)=4f(1)), gives no reason for option (A) beyond 'might not be one-one' (no counterexample), and checks option (B) only for n=1,2,3 without showing f(1)=1. Completed: induction f(n)=n f(1), explicit counterexample for (A), and the proof that onto forces f(1)=1. The answer (A) is unchanged.
useful_results: If $f\circ g$ is one-one then $g$ is one-one; if $f\circ g$ is onto then $f$ is onto. The converses (and the other directions) are false in general.
$f(n+1)=f(n)+c$ on $\mathbb N$ gives an arithmetic progression $f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)c$; with $c=f(1)$ this is $f(n)=nf(1)$.
To show 'if P then Q' is false, one counterexample (a non-injective onto $g$ such as $\lceil n/2\rceil$) is enough.

concepts: Composition of piecewise-defined functions on $\mathbb N$
One-one and onto functions
questions.question: Let $\mathbb N$ be the set of natural numbers and two functions $f$ and $g$ be defined as $f,g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that $f(n)=\begin{cases}\frac{n+1}{2}&\text{if }n\text{ is odd}\\\frac n2&\text{if }n\text{ is even}\end{cases}$ and $g(n)=n-(-1)^n$. Then $f\circ g$ is:
questions.key_idea: $g$ swaps $2k-1\leftrightarrow2k$ (a bijection), so $f\circ g$ has exactly the same one-one/onto behaviour as $f$.
solution: For odd $n$: $g(n)=n-(-1)^n=n+1$, which is even, so $f(g(n))=f(n+1)=\frac{n+1}{2}$.
For even $n$: $g(n)=n-1$, which is odd, so $f(g(n))=f(n-1)=\frac{(n-1)+1}{2}=\frac n2$.
Hence $f\circ g$ is onto but not one-one.
questions.correction_note: The PDF gives only the answer key (C) with no working for this question; the solution above was written from scratch and checked numerically for n = 1..12.

alternate_solutions.idea: $g$ is a bijection (an involution swapping $2k-1\leftrightarrow2k$), so $f\circ g$ inherits the properties of $f$.
solution: $g(2k-1)=2k$ and $g(2k)=2k-1$, so $g\circ g=\mathrm{id}$; hence $g$ is a bijection of $\mathbb N$.
Composing with a bijection on the right does not change the range or the fibre sizes: $f\circ g$ is onto iff $f$ is onto, and one-one iff $f$ is one-one.
$f(2m)=m$ for every $m\in\mathbb N$, so $f$ is onto.
Therefore $f\circ g$ is onto but not one-one.

useful_results: If $g$ is a bijection then $f\circ g$ is one-one iff $f$ is one-one, and onto iff $f$ is onto.
$f(n)=\lceil n/2\rceil$ (odd $\to\frac{n+1}2$, even $\to\frac n2$) is a standard onto, two-to-one map $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$.
$n-(-1)^n$ swaps consecutive pairs $(1,2),(3,4),\dots$ - a common bijection used in such questions.

concepts: Counting functions $g$ satisfying $g\circ f=f$
questions.question: Let $A=\{1,2,3,\dots,10\}$ and $f:A\to A$ be defined as $f(k)=\begin{cases}k+1&\text{if }k\text{ is odd}\\k&\text{if }k\text{ is even}\end{cases}$. Then the number of possible functions $g:A\to A$ such that $g\circ f=f$ is:
questions.key_idea: $g\circ f=f$ only constrains $g$ on the range of $f$ (the even numbers), where $g$ must be the identity; the other values are free.
solution: $g(f(x))=f(x)$ for all $x\in A$ means $g(y)=y$ for every $y$ in the range of $f$.
So $g(x)=x$ when $x$ is even: $g(2)=2,\ g(4)=4,\dots,g(10)=10$ - one way.
For each of the 5 odd inputs $1,3,5,7,9$, $g$ is unrestricted: 10 choices each.
useful_results: $g\circ f=f$ forces $g=\mathrm{id}$ on $\mathrm{Range}(f)$ and leaves $g$ free elsewhere: count $=|A|^{|A|-|\mathrm{Range}f|}$.
The number of $g:A\to A$ with $g\circ f=h$ is $0$ unless $h$ is constant on each fibre of $f$; if it is, $g$ is fixed on $\mathrm{Range}(f)$ and the count is again $|A|^{|A|-|\mathrm{Range}f|}$.
Check on a small analogue: for $A=\{1,\dots,6\}$ the same rule gives $6^3=216$ (confirmed by brute force).

concepts: Telescoping sum of inverse tangents and its limit
questions.question: Let $S_k=\sum_{r=1}^{k}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6^r}{2^{2r+1}+3^{2r+1}}\right)$. Then $\lim_{k\to\infty}S_k$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Divide numerator and denominator by $2^{2r+1}$ to see $\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ with $a=\left(\frac32\right)^{r+1}$, $b=\left(\frac32\right)^r$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each term is an argument difference: $\arg\left[(2^{r+1}+i3^{r+1})\overline{(2^r+i3^r)}\right]$ equals the term, so the sum is a difference of two arguments.
solution: The imaginary part is $6^r(3-2)=6^r$, so $z_{r+1}\overline{z_r}=(2^{2r+1}+3^{2r+1})+i\,6^r$ (real part positive).
As $k\to\infty$, $\arg z_{k+1}\to\frac\pi2$, so the limit is $\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}\frac32=\cot^{-1}\frac32$.

useful_results: $\tan^{-1}a-\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ whenever $ab>-1$: a term $\tan^{-1}\frac{u-v}{1+uv}$ telescopes if $u=h(r+1),v=h(r)$.
Here $h(r)=\left(\frac32\right)^r$: $\frac{h(r+1)-h(r)}{1+h(r+1)h(r)}=\frac{6^r}{2^{2r+1}+3^{2r+1}}$ - a geometric $h$ is the natural choice when the denominator has the form $a^{2r+1}+b^{2r+1}$.
Complex-number view: $\tan^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{Im}}{\mathrm{Re}}$ of $z_{r+1}\overline{z_r}$ is $\arg z_{r+1}-\arg z_r$ (valid when the real part is positive).
$\tan^{-1}t\to\frac\pi2$ as $t\to\infty$, and $\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}t=\cot^{-1}t$ for $t>0$.

concepts: Left-hand and right-hand limits with greatest integer and modulus functions
questions.question: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer $\le t$. If for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R-\{0,1\}$, $\lim_{x\to0}\left|\frac{1-x+|x|}{\lambda-x+[x]}\right|=L$, then $L$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The limit exists only if the left and right limits agree; near $0$, $[x]=-1$ on the left and $0$ on the right.
solution: The limit exists, so LHL $=$ RHL $=L$.
useful_results: At an integer point $a$: $[x]=a-1$ for $x\to a^-$ and $[x]=a$ for $x\to a^+$ - always split into two one-sided limits.
$|\lambda|=|\lambda-1|$ means $\lambda$ is equidistant from $0$ and $1$, so $\lambda=\frac12$ (the midpoint).
Existence of a limit with the condition on a parameter is equivalent to equating one-sided limits.

concepts: Telescoping sum of $\cot^{-1}$ with sum of even numbers
questions.question: The value of $\cot\left(\sum_{n=1}^{19}\cot^{-1}\left(1+\sum_{p=1}^{n}2p\right)\right)$ is:

alternate_solutions.idea: Use complex arguments: $(1+i(n+1))\overline{(1+in)}=1+n(n+1)+i$, so each term is $\arg(1+i(n+1))-\arg(1+in)$.

useful_results: $\sum_{p=1}^{n}2p=n(n+1)$; $1+n(n+1)$ is the classical telescoping denominator: $\cot^{-1}(1+n(n+1))=\tan^{-1}(n+1)-\tan^{-1}n$.
Generally $\cot^{-1}(1+d\,n(n+d))$-type or $\tan^{-1}\frac{d}{1+n(n+d)}=\tan^{-1}(n+d)-\tan^{-1}n$ telescopes with step $d$.
$\tan^{-1}a-\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ (for $ab>-1$); then $\cot$ of the total angle is just the reciprocal of its tangent.
Argument of a product is the sum of arguments, so telescoping sums of $\tan^{-1}$ can be read as arguments of products of complex numbers.

concepts: Limit with a $\frac{1-\cos}{x^2}$ standard form and root condition
Greatest integer of a one-sided limit
questions.question: Let $x=2$ be a root of the equation $x^2+px+q=0$ and $f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1-\cos(x^2-4px+q^2+8q+16)}{(x-2p)^4}&,x\neq2p\\0&,x=2p\end{cases}$. Then $\lim_{x\to2p^+}[f(x)]$, where $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function, is:
questions.key_idea: $x=2$ root gives $q+4=-2p$, so the cosine argument is exactly $(x-2p)^2$; then $f\to\frac12$ from below, so $[f]=0$.
solution: Since $1-\cos u<\frac{u^2}{2}$ for $u\neq0$, we have $0<f(x)<\frac12$ near $2p$, so $[f(x)]=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF line 'lim 1/2 {(2p+h)^2 - 4p(2p+h) + q^2 + 82 + 16}/h^2}^2 = 1/2' has a typo (82 instead of 8q) and the factor (2p+h)^2-4p(2p+h)+(q+4)^2 = h^2 only after using q+4=-2p, which the PDF does not state. It then jumps from 'limit = 1/2' to 'lim [f(x)] = 0' without saying why the floor is 0: the limit 1/2 is approached from below, so f < 1/2 and [f] = 0. Both steps added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $1-\cos u=2\sin^2\frac u2$: $f=\frac12\left(\frac{\sin(u/2)}{u/2}\right)^2$ with $\frac{\sin t}{t}\in(0,1)$, so $0<f<\frac12$ on a punctured neighbourhood with no limit computation.
solution: As before, the root condition gives $f(x)=\frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}$ with $u=(x-2p)^2>0$ near $2p$.
For $0<t<\pi$, $0<\frac{\sin t}{t}<1$; with $t=\frac u2$ small and positive, $0<f<\frac12$.
So $[f(x)]=0$ for all $x$ near (and different from) $2p$, and the one-sided limit is $0$.

useful_results: $\lim_{u\to0}\frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}=\frac12$, and $1-\cos u<\frac{u^2}{2}$ for $u\neq0$ - so the value $\frac12$ is approached from below.

For $\lim[f(x)]$ do not stop at the limit of $f$: if the limit is an integer $N$, the answer depends on the side ($N-1$ from below, $N$ from above); if not, it is $\lfloor\text{limit}\rfloor$. Here $f\to\frac12$, so the answer is $0$.
If $x_0$ is a root of $x^2+px+q$, use $q=-x_0^2-px_0$ to simplify any expression of the form $x^2-2ax+(\dots)^2$ into a perfect square.

concepts: Non-differentiability of $\max\{|x|,x^2\}$ and of a piecewise function at its junctions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}\max\{|x|,x^2\}&,|x|\le2\\8-2|x|&,2<|x|\le4\end{cases}$. Let $S$ be the set of points in the interval $(-4,4)$ at which $f$ is not differentiable. Then $S$:
questions.key_idea: Draw the graph: $\max\{|x|,x^2\}$ has corners where $|x|$ meets $x^2$ ($0,\pm1$), plus the junctions $\pm2$.
solution: On $[-2,2]$: $|x|\ge x^2$ for $|x|\le1$ and $x^2\ge|x|$ for $1\le|x|\le2$, so $f=|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ and $f=x^2$ on $1\le|x|\le2$.
At $x=0$: $f=|x|$ has a corner (slopes $-1$ and $1$). Not differentiable.
At $x=\pm1$: slopes change from $\pm1$ (of $|x|$) to $\pm2$ (of $x^2$); e.g. at $x=1$: left slope $1$, right slope $2x=2$. Not differentiable.
At $x=2$: $f=x^2$ on the left (value $4$, slope $4$); $f=8-2x$ on the right (value $4$, slope $-2$). Continuous but not differentiable. Same at $x=-2$ by symmetry.
Everywhere else $f$ is a polynomial piece, hence differentiable.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's first line writes the domain of the first branch as '|x| >= 2' (typo; the question and the next line have |x| <= 2), and then just reads the non-differentiable points off a sketch without any slope check. I added the analytic slope comparison at 0, +-1, +-2; the answer (C) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $f$ is even, so check $x\ge0$ only; $\max\{g,h\}$ of two differentiable functions is non-differentiable exactly where $g=h$ with $g'\neq h'$.
solution: On $[0,2]$ the two functions $|x|=x$ and $x^2$ are differentiable except at $|x|$'s corner $x=0$; they cross where $x=x^2$, i.e. $x=0,1$.
At $x=1$: slopes $1\neq2$, so a corner. At $x=0$: $|x|$ itself has a corner, so $f$ is not differentiable there.
At the junction $x=2$: left derivative $2x=4$, right derivative $-2$, not equal. For $2<x<4$, $f=8-2x$ is linear (differentiable).
Non-differentiable points for $x\ge0$: $0,1,2$; by evenness add $-1,-2$. So $S=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$.

useful_results: $\max\{g(x),h(x)\}$ (or $\min$) of differentiable functions is non-differentiable exactly at crossing points where $g'\neq h'$; where they touch tangentially it stays differentiable.
At a junction of pieces, a function is differentiable iff it is continuous and the two one-sided derivatives agree; compare both value and slope.
If $f$ is even, a point $x_0\neq0$ is non-differentiable iff $-x_0$ is; check $x_0=0$ separately ($|x|$-like pieces give a corner).

concepts: Sum of a grouped series and rationalisation of the difference of square roots
questions.question: The value of $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1+2-3+4+5-6+\dots+(3n-2)+(3n-1)-3n}{\sqrt{2n^4+4n+3}-\sqrt{n^4+5n+4}}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Group the numerator in triples: $(3r-2)+(3r-1)-3r=3(r-1)$; then rationalise the denominator.
solution: Rationalise the denominator: multiply by $\left(\sqrt{2n^4+4n+3}+\sqrt{n^4+5n+4}\right)$; the denominator becomes $(2n^4+4n+3)-(n^4+5n+4)=n^4-n-1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF rewrites the denominator as sqrt(2n^4+3n+1) - sqrt(n^4+n+3) (the printed paper has 4n+3 and 5n+4) and later uses 3n-1 / n+3; its conjugate step therefore uses wrong lower-order terms. These lower-order terms do not affect the limit, so the final value 3/2(sqrt2+1) and key B stand; the working above uses the paper's actual denominator.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare leading orders only: numerator $\sim\frac32n^2$ and denominator $\sim(\sqrt2-1)n^2$ (no cancellation of leading terms, so no rationalisation needed).
solution: The leading coefficients $\sqrt2$ and $1$ are different, so the difference is $\sim(\sqrt2-1)n^2$ with no cancellation.

useful_results: A difference of two square roots whose leading terms differ ($\sqrt{a}\,n^k-\sqrt{b}\,n^k$, $a\neq b$) behaves like $(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)n^k$; rationalise only when the leading terms cancel.
Pattern sums: $(3r-2)+(3r-1)-3r=3r-3$; always group a repeating sign pattern of period $m$ into blocks.

concepts: Limit of $\left(\sum a_k^m\right)^{1/m}$ as the exponent tends to infinity
questions.question: $\lim_{t\to0}\left(1^{\frac1{\sin^2t}}+2^{\frac1{\sin^2t}}+\dots+n^{\frac1{\sin^2t}}\right)^{\sin^2t}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: With $m=\frac1{\sin^2t}\to\infty$ the largest term $n^m$ dominates: $(\sum k^m)^{1/m}\to n$.
solution: Raise to the power $\sin^2t=\frac1m$: the prefactor gives $(n^m)^{1/m}=n$.
The bracket therefore tends to $1+0=1$, and $[1]^{\sin^2t}\to1^0=1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the prefactor as '1/n^{sin^2 t}' (it should be n^{cosec^2 t}, which gives n after the outer power sin^2 t). The final value n is correct. Notation fixed; the argument is the same.

alternate_solutions.idea: Squeeze: $n^m\le\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^m\le n\cdot n^m$, then take $m$-th roots.
solution: With $m=\frac1{\sin^2t}>0$: the largest term is $n^m$, so $n^m\le\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^m$.
Each of the $n$ terms is $\le n^m$, so $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^m\le n\cdot n^m$.
Raise to the power $\frac1m=\sin^2t>0$: $n\le\left(\sum k^m\right)^{1/m}\le n\cdot n^{1/m}$.
As $t\to0$, $m\to\infty$ and $n^{1/m}=n^{\sin^2t}\to1$; the right bound $\to n$.
By the sandwich theorem the limit is $n$.

useful_results: $\lim_{m\to\infty}\left(a_1^m+\dots+a_n^m\right)^{1/m}=\max a_i$ for positive $a_i$ (the $\ell^p$-norm tends to the sup-norm).
For the integral analogue, $\left(\int f^m\right)^{1/m}\to\max|f|$.
The same squeeze gives $\lim\sqrt[n]{a^n+b^n}=\max\{a,b\}$.

concepts: Maximum and minimum of modulus functions and evaluation of a rational limit
questions.question: Let $f(x)=5-|x-2|$ and $g(x)=|x+1|$, $x\in\mathbb R$. If $f(x)$ attains maximum value at $\alpha$ and $g(x)$ attains minimum value at $\beta$, then $\lim_{x\to-\alpha\beta}\frac{(x-1)(x^2-5x+6)}{x^2-6x+8}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\alpha=2$ (peak of $5-|x-2|$) and $\beta=-1$ (vertex of $|x+1|$) give $-\alpha\beta=2$, the root of the common factor $(x-2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: L'Hopital's rule on the $\frac00$ form at $x=2$.
solution: With $x\to2$: numerator $N=(x-1)(x^2-5x+6)\to0$ and denominator $D=x^2-6x+8\to0$, a $\frac00$ form.

useful_results: $a-|x-p|$ has maximum $a$ at $x=p$; $|x-p|+c$ has minimum $c$ at $x=p$.
For a rational $\frac00$ limit at $x=a$, cancel the common factor $(x-a)$, or use $\lim=\frac{N'(a)}{D'(a)}$ if $D'(a)\neq0$.
Read the limit point carefully ($-\alpha\beta$, not $\alpha\beta$): here it equals $2$.

concepts: Reciprocal conjugate surds and equations of the form $u^t+u^{-t}=c$
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x:x\in\mathbb R\text{ and }\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)^{x^2-4}+\left(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\right)^{x^2-4}=10\right\}$. Then $n(S)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Square the bases: $(5+2\sqrt6)(5-2\sqrt6)=1$ and the sum is $10$, so the equation holds exactly when $\frac{x^2-4}2=\pm1$.
solution: So the equation $u^t+u^{-t}=10=u+u^{-1}$ (with $u=5+2\sqrt6$) holds when $t=\pm1$, i.e. $\frac{x^2-4}{2}=\pm1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Hyperbolic cosine: $u^t+u^{-t}=2\cosh(t\ln u)$ is even and strictly increasing for $t>0$, so it is injective in $|t|$.
solution: Let $u=5+2\sqrt6$, $t=\frac{x^2-4}{2}$; the equation is $u^t+u^{-t}=10$, i.e. $2\cosh(t\ln u)=10$.
Since $u+u^{-1}=10$, $2\cosh(\ln u)=10$ too, so $\cosh(t\ln u)=\cosh(\ln u)$.
$\cosh$ is even and strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, so $|t\ln u|=\ln u$, i.e. $|t|=1$ (as $\ln u>0$).
$\frac{x^2-4}{2}=\pm1$ gives $x^2=6$ or $x^2=2$: four real values $\pm\sqrt6,\pm\sqrt2$, so $n(S)=4$.

useful_results: $(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^2=a+b+2\sqrt{ab}$; conjugate surds $p\pm q$ with $p^2-q^2=1$ are reciprocals, so $u^t+u^{-t}$ is symmetric in $t\leftrightarrow-t$.
For $u>1$, $u^t+u^{-t}$ is even in $t$ and strictly increasing in $|t|$, so $u^t+u^{-t}=u+u^{-1}$ has exactly the two roots $t=\pm1$.
$\left(\sqrt3\pm\sqrt2\right)^2=5\pm2\sqrt6$ and $(5+2\sqrt6)+(5-2\sqrt6)=10$ - a standard JEE pair.

concepts: Multiplicative functional equation $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ and geometric series
questions.question: Let $\sum_{k=1}^{10}f(a+k)=16\left(2^{10}-1\right)$, where the function $f$ satisfies $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ for all natural numbers $x,y$ and $f(1)=2$. Then the natural number $a$ is:
questions.key_idea: $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ with $f(1)=2$ gives $f(x)=2^x$ on $\mathbb N$, turning the sum into a geometric series.
useful_results: On $\mathbb N$: $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ and $f(1)=c$ give $f(n)=c^n$ (induction on $f(n+1)=f(n)f(1)$).
$\sum_{k=1}^{n}c^{a+k}=c^{a}\cdot\frac{c(c^n-1)}{c-1}$; for $c=2$ it is $2^{a+1}(2^n-1)$ - compare with the given $16(2^{10}-1)=2^{4}(2^{10}-1)$ to read off $a+1=4$.
Recognise $16=2^4$ and match powers of 2 before computing anything.
